title: Local Delivery Service
prompt: Design a local courier service that matches packages with available couriers in real-time. The system should support package pickup and delivery within a city. Target ~50k daily deliveries with same-day service, real-time courier location tracking, and estimated arrival times.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements for this system?
stages.howToAnswer: List 3-5 'Users should be able to...' statements covering the must-have behavior. Separate customer, courier, and admin flows. Skip nice-to-haves like payment processing or customer reviews unless explicitly asked.

exampleHints.headline: Example (DoorDash):
bullets: Customers can place an order and track its status
Drivers can accept deliveries and update their location

must: Customers can submit a package and request delivery
Couriers can view available deliveries and accept them
Customers can track delivery status and courier location in real-time
should: Couriers can update delivery status (picked up, delivered)
System suggests pickup and delivery windows
avoid: Drifting into payment processing, returns, or customer reviews
Including admin dashboards unless explicitly asked

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Customers should be able to submit a package and request a delivery within their city.
2. Couriers should be able to view available deliveries and accept them.
3. Customers should be able to track their delivery status and see the courier's real-time location.
4. Couriers should be able to mark packages as picked up and delivered.
hints: Two sides: customer and courier. What can each do with a package?
Real-time is a key phrase — what visibility does each side need?
Stay focused on delivery operations. Skip billing, returns, and ratings.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?
stages.howToAnswer: Cover latency targets (ETA accuracy, location updates), availability, scale (deliveries/day, concurrent couriers), and real-time constraints. Quantify each requirement.

must: Low latency matching — match courier to package in <5 seconds
Real-time location updates — push updates every 5–10 seconds
Scale: ~50k daily deliveries, ~2k concurrent couriers
High availability — 99.9% uptime for matching and tracking
should: ETA accuracy — within 5 minutes
Durability — delivery records must not be lost
avoid: Conflating latency targets (matching vs ETA vs location updates)

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Matching latency: <5 seconds from package creation to courier assignment.
- Location updates: every 5–10 seconds to customers and dispatch system.
- Scale: ~50k deliveries/day = ~2 RPS average, ~600 RPS peak; ~2k concurrent couriers.
- Availability: 99.9% uptime for matching and location tracking.
- ETA accuracy: ±5 minutes.
- Durability: all delivery records must be persisted and recoverable after failure.
hints: Matching is the critical path. What latency budget does matching have, and what does tracking need?
Location updates are different from matching — what's the frequency, and why?
Quantify the load: deliveries/day, concurrent couriers, and RPS.

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core entities of this system?
stages.howToAnswer: List the nouns. Package, Courier, Delivery, Location. Don't define schemas yet — that comes in High-Level Design.

must: Package — the item to be delivered
Courier — the person making the delivery
Delivery — the assignment of a package to a courier
should: Location — real-time position of a courier
DeliveryStatus — history of state changes (pending, picked up, delivered)
avoid: Inventing entities the requirements don't justify

hints: What are the three main actors or artifacts in the system?
Which entity represents the live state of a courier, and which is historical?

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: One endpoint per functional requirement. REST is the default — show method, path, request body shape, and response.

must: POST endpoint to create a delivery request
GET endpoint to track delivery status
POST endpoint for courier to accept a delivery
POST endpoint to update delivery status (pickup, delivery)
should: GET endpoint to list available deliveries for a courier
Webhooks or polling for location updates
Returns appropriate HTTP status codes
avoid: Mixing multiple concerns in one endpoint

hints: Start with the two key actions: submitting a delivery and accepting it.
Customers need to see status and location; couriers need a list of nearby deliveries.
Distinguish state-change endpoints (accept, status update) from read endpoints (track, list).

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the high-level architecture. Walk through each endpoint.
stages.howToAnswer: Boxes and arrows: mobile clients → load balancer → API service → database. Add a matching service, location cache, and real-time messaging. Walk through the matching flow (how does a package find a courier?) and the tracking flow.

must: Client / Load balancer / API service / Database
Matching algorithm or strategy (e.g., nearest courier, availability check)
Real-time location tracking mechanism (WebSocket, gRPC, or polling)
should: Location cache for hot courier positions
Message queue for asynchronous status updates
Geospatial index (e.g., quadtree, R-tree) for fast nearest-neighbor lookup
Schema: Delivery, Courier, Location entities
avoid: Not addressing how location updates reach customers in real-time

stages.sampleAnswer:
Architecture:
- Mobile app (customer & courier) ↔ ALB
- API service (stateless, deployed on multiple AZs)
- Matching service (subscribes to location updates, performs geospatial queries)
- Location service (maintains in-memory cache of courier positions, broadcasts updates via WebSocket to customers)
- PostgreSQL + PostGIS for delivery history and package metadata
- Redis for hot location cache (courier ID → lat/lng + timestamp)
- Kafka for location updates and status-change events

Matching flow:
1. Customer submits delivery request via POST /deliveries.
2. API validates address and price, writes to DB.
3. Matching service queries Redis for couriers within 5km radius, sorts by distance + acceptance rate.
4. Sends notification (push or polling) to top 3 couriers in parallel.
5. First acceptance wins; other offers are retracted.
6. Delivery is assigned; customer sees courier info and WebSocket-streamed location.

Location flow:
1. Courier app sends location every 10 seconds to location service.
2. Location service updates Redis and publishes event to Kafka.
3. Kafka topic triggers push notifications or WebSocket updates to relevant customers.
hints: Matching is the headline trick. How do you find the nearest available courier without scanning the entire database?
Location updates must flow to customers in real-time. What's the channel: WebSocket, polling, or both?
Geospatial indexing is key — what data structure lets you find couriers near a destination in <100ms?

deepDives.title: Sub-5-second matching
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you match a package to a courier in under 5 seconds, even with thousands of couriers?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: 1. Maintain an in-memory geospatial index of all available couriers (Redis with geospatial commands, or a local quadtree). 2. On package creation, query the index for couriers within 5km, sorted by distance. 3. Send parallel notifications to the top 3; first to accept wins. 4. Write the assignment to DB in the background. If the matching service's local index is out-of-date (stale by <30s), acceptable — a slightly suboptimal match is better than missing the SLO. For fault tolerance, replicate the matching service so a failure doesn't block all matches.

must: In-memory geospatial index (not a DB scan)
Concrete data structure or service (Redis geo, quadtree, etc.)
Parallel notification strategy to reduce acceptance latency
should: Handling of stale index
Fault tolerance for the matching service

hints: A full database scan is too slow. What in-memory structure pre-computes nearby couriers?
Sending notifications is slow too. Should you send to one courier or a few in parallel?
Your index becomes stale — is that acceptable, and at what staleness threshold does it break the system?

deepDives.title: Real-time location tracking
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you push courier location updates to customers in real-time without overwhelming your system?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: 1. Couriers send location every 10 seconds to a location service (or directly to a WebSocket gateway). 2. Location service batches updates (e.g., collect 100 updates, send every 1 second) to reduce network traffic. 3. Push to customers via WebSocket for active connections; fall back to polling or push notifications for inactive sessions. 4. Store location history in a time-series DB (e.g., InfluxDB, Cassandra) for analytics and reconciliation. 5. Use geohashing to partition the location stream so no single process becomes a bottleneck.

must: Identify the push mechanism (WebSocket, polling, or hybrid)
Batching or aggregation strategy to avoid message explosion
should: Time-series storage for history
Fallback for inactive connections
Partitioning strategy for scale
avoid: Pushing every location update to every customer (will saturate the network)

hints: Sending every courier update to every customer is too much. What's a reasonable batching strategy?
Not all customers are actively watching. How do you handle the difference between active and inactive sessions?
At thousands of concurrent deliveries, a single WebSocket server can't handle all location updates. How do you partition?

deepDives.title: Availability under failures
deepDives.questionPrompt: What happens if the matching service crashes, or the location cache is lost? How does the system stay available?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Matching service: stateless, replicated behind a load balancer across 3 AZs. On crash, traffic reroutes to replicas in <5s. The geospatial index is rebuilt from the location cache on startup (warm recovery in <10s). Location cache (Redis): multi-AZ replication with automatic failover. If the entire Redis node is lost, locations fall back to querying the last-known position from the database (latency increases to ~100ms, but no outage). Delivery operations use an idempotent protocol: re-sending a match or status update is safe because both the DB and Kafka record the source ID and timestamp.

must: Identify the critical component
Concrete failover or replication plan
should: Graceful degradation (e.g., slower but still available)
Idempotency to handle retries
avoid: Single points of failure left unaddressed

hints: What's the most critical component? If it goes down, what does the system fall back to?
When the matching service crashes, how does it recover its geospatial index? Is rebuilding fast enough?
If the location cache is lost, is location tracking completely unavailable, or degraded?
